article:
## LinkedIn swapped its AI writer for a proofreader

LinkedIn has rolled out a feature called **Post Proofreader** for eligible Premium members. It replaces the AI powered "post enhancement" option, the button that used to rewrite your draft for you, which LinkedIn removed the month before.

The difference sounds small. It isn't.

## What Post Proofreader actually does

According to LinkedIn, the tool "helps eligible Premium members improve post drafts before publishing." You see suggested changes before anything is applied, with inline change tracking, so you can check what changed and decide whether to keep it.

The options focus on three jobs:

- reviewing spelling, grammar and punctuation
- shortening a post while keeping its meaning
- improving clarity

What it no longer does is generate a post that didn't start with you. Social Media Today framed it well: the shift is about improving post language, not producing an idea that didn't originate from the person posting.

## Why LinkedIn made the change

The context is the "AI slop" backlash. LinkedIn added an option for members to report content they believe is low quality AI output. Less than three weeks after launch, that option had been used **more than one million times**. In September, LinkedIn extended reporting to comments as well.

So the platform is sending a fairly clear signal. Generated posts are a reputational risk for LinkedIn. Polished human posts are what it wants more of.

## What this means for marketers and founders

If you run a personal brand, a founder account or an employee advocacy programme, this matters in three ways:

1. **The tools are moving towards editing, not authoring.** Expect more features like this, and fewer "write it for me" buttons, on the platform itself.
2. **Readers are now actively flagging content.** A post that reads as generic can now get reported, not just ignored.
3. **Voice becomes the differentiator.** When everyone can produce clean text, the specific opinion, story or number is what earns attention.

I'll admit the limit here: LinkedIn hasn't said how reports affect reach, so I wouldn't claim it punishes AI writing. What we know is that members are reporting it in large numbers, and LinkedIn is redesigning its own tools around that.

## What I'd do

- **Write the first draft yourself.** Voice notes work. Bullet points work. It just has to be your thinking.
- **Use AI for the second pass only.** Ask for grammar fixes, a shorter version, or a clarity check. Keep your wording.
- **Read the tracked changes.** If a suggestion makes you sound like everyone else, reject it.
- **Brief your ghostwriters and agencies the same way.** Their job is to sharpen the founder's voice, not replace it.
- **Keep one specific detail in every post.** A real number, a real moment, a real opinion. That's the part no tool can supply.

From my own work across 850+ creator deals, the content that travelled was rarely the most polished. It was the most specific. LinkedIn seems to be betting on the same thing.

article:
## Instagram's Edits app now reads your numbers for you

On 30 September, Instagram announced an AI video assistant inside **Edits**, its video editing app. It's a chat assistant, but the selling point isn't editing. It's analysis.

## What the Edits assistant does

Brett Westervelt, who leads Edits, described it like this: the assistant knows your account's Instagram metrics, "things like follows, views, video retention, likes, shares," and combines them with your comments, what's trending on Instagram and what your audience is into. He said it can spot patterns in performance over time and surface insights that are hard to see from the metrics alone.

From there, it suggests what to make next. PetaPixel summed it up as an assistant that analyses your Reels and suggests new ideas.

## The pitch: analysis, not authorship

The most interesting line from Instagram is about what the tool won't do. Westervelt said creators consistently told the team they want "a tool that handles the analysis, not one that does the creative work for them." His summary: "Edits assistant does the digging for you. The creative calls are still yours."

That matches what LinkedIn did with its proofreader. Platforms are learning that audiences push back on content that feels generated. So the AI is moving behind the scenes, into data and planning.

## The catch

- **It's capped.** Creators hit a usage limit and can get more with a Meta One subscription.
- **It only sees Instagram.** The assistant works from your Instagram data. Your TikTok or YouTube performance isn't part of the picture.
- **Suggestions are still guesses.** Patterns in past data don't guarantee the next video works. Treat ideas as hypotheses to test.

Meta first previewed the assistant in June at an invite-only creator event, and TechCrunch notes YouTube is working on its own conversational editing tool for early next year. Expect this to become standard.

## Why this matters for brands

Having worked on 850+ creator deals, I'd always rather see a creator's retention and share data than a follower count. Followers tell you reach. Retention tells you whether people actually watched.

If creators get an assistant that turns their own stats into clear insight, two things change:

1. Creator pitches get sharper, with reasons for each content idea.
2. Brand briefs that ignore the creator's data will look lazy by comparison.

## What I'd do

- **Creators:** ask the assistant one question a week: "Which of my last 10 Reels kept people watching longest, and what did they have in common?" Then make one video that tests the answer.
- **Brands and agencies:** ask creators to share what their assistant suggests before you send a brief. Build the brief around their audience, not your mood board.
- **Everyone:** keep the creative call human. Use the data to choose the topic. Use your taste to make it.

## Sources

- [TechCrunch: Instagram rolls out an AI video assistant for creators (30 Sep 2026)](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/30/instagram-rolls-out-an-ai-video-assistant-for-creators/)
- [PetaPixel: Instagram launches AI assistant that analyzes your Reels and suggests new ideas (1 Oct 2026)](https://petapixel.com/2026/10/01/instagram-launches-ai-assistant-that-analyzes-your-reels-and-suggests-new-ideas/)

article:
## OpenAI's Dots: agents that don't wait for you

At DevDay on 29 September, OpenAI launched **Dots**, a set of always-on AI agents inside ChatGPT. The idea is simple: instead of prompting ChatGPT one task at a time, you give an agent a goal and it keeps moving the work forward.

## How Dots work

Based on OpenAI's announcement and SiliconANGLE's coverage:

- **Powered by GPT-6 Astra.**
- **Its own cloud computer.** Each agent works on a machine you can open at any time to see what it is doing.
- **4,000+ apps.** More than 4,000 apps are reachable through OpenAI's plugins. With permission, an agent can also work directly on your laptop.
- **Where you talk to it.** ChatGPT on desktop, web or mobile, plus Slack and Teams. Context follows the agent between channels.
- **It learns your preferences** from feedback, and OpenAI says some work will show up before anyone asks for it.

## The safety rails

When nobody has given it a task, a Dot does what OpenAI calls proactive research. During that time, its app connections are read-only, so it can't send messages or change anything. Actions that could touch your accounts or share information must pass a check called auto-review. And OpenAI itself tells users to review consequential work because the agents "can still make mistakes."

One example in the coverage: an early tester had forgotten to bill a client. His agent noticed, prepared the invoice and waited for approval before sending it. That's the pattern to copy. Agent prepares, human approves.

## Who gets it, and who doesn't

Dots began rolling out to ChatGPT **Pro and Business Premium** subscribers. One agent is included at no extra cost. More agents and more capacity are planned later, at prices OpenAI hasn't disclosed.

The catch for my European readers: **Pro subscribers in the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK are not included.** Enterprise customers can try a beta once an admin switches it on.

## Why marketers should care

Most marketing work is a chain of small, repeatable steps: pull the numbers, spot the change, draft the update, chase the approval. That's exactly the shape of work an always-on agent is built for. The question isn't whether agents will touch marketing ops. It's whether your processes are written down clearly enough for one to follow.

## What I'd do

- **Write the job description first.** One goal, the apps it can touch, and what it must never do alone.
- **Start read-only.** Reporting and research before anything that sends, posts or spends.
- **Define approval points.** Anything customer-facing or money-related gets a human check. Always.
- **Pick a boring task.** Weekly campaign summaries are a better first job than brand strategy.
- **If you're in Europe,** use the waiting time to document your workflows. That's the work that makes agents useful later.

I'm honest about my limit here: I haven't used Dots myself yet. This is based on the launch details, not hands-on testing.

## Sources

- [SiliconANGLE: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on AI agents in ChatGPT with their own cloud computers (29 Sep 2026)](https://siliconangle.com/2026/09/29/openai-launches-dots-always-on-ai-agents-in-chatgpt-with-their-own-cloud-computers/)
- [OpenAI: Introducing Dots](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/)

article:
## Meta takes Muse to small businesses

On 29 September, Meta announced **Muse for Small Business**, a version of its Muse AI agent that connects to the software owners already use to run their companies. Muse itself launched on 8 September for users in the US and Canada as a personal assistant.

## What it connects to

According to Meta's announcement, as reported by The Next Web:

- **Commerce and money:** Shopify, Stripe and Intuit's QuickBooks, among others
- **Design:** Canva
- **Meta's own tools:** analytics from Instagram business accounts and Facebook Pages, plus Meta ad accounts
- **Work apps:** Slack, Zoom, Notion, Figma and Dropbox
- **Custom connectors** for services Meta doesn't support yet

With those connections, Muse can draw on a company's brand, shop, accounts and customer records. Reuters reported that owners can ask it to analyse sales, campaigns and social activity, develop a growth plan, draft customer communications, and create ads and other content.

## The approval rule

Meta said the agent will not post content, send messages or buy anything without the owner's approval. That's the most important line in the announcement. It turns Muse into a drafting and analysis assistant with a human sign-off, not an autopilot.

## Why Meta is doing this

Meta's Vishal Shah told Axios that roughly **one in three** people who tried Muse early had already connected it to a business account of some kind. "People are using Muse to run their business," he said. In other words, owners were already doing this informally. Meta is making it official.

Most people can use Muse at no cost, with paid plans offering higher usage limits.

## What it means for marketers

For a small business, the appeal is obvious: one assistant that can see your sales, your social stats and your ad account in the same conversation. The usual problem with small business marketing isn't a lack of tools. It's that nobody has time to join the dots between them.

The risk is just as obvious. An agent that drafts ads from your data will reflect the quality of your inputs. If your positioning is fuzzy, it will produce fuzzy ads at scale.

## What I'd do

- **Write a one-page brand brief first.** Who you sell to, what you promise, three words for your tone, and words you never use.
- **Start with analysis, not creation.** Ask it what changed in sales and campaigns this month before you ask it for new ads.
- **Keep approval as a habit.** Read every draft as if a junior wrote it. Because, in effect, one did.
- **Check what it can see.** Connect only the accounts it needs for the job.
- **Compare against a human version.** Run one AI-drafted ad next to one you wrote, and let the numbers decide.

My limit: Muse is available in the US and Canada, and I haven't tested the business version myself. These are the launch details, plus how I'd approach any new marketing agent.

## Sources

article:
## TikTok's plan: close the sale inside the feed

At Advertising Week New York 2026, TikTok unveiled a package of AI driven advertising and commerce products. Taken together, they point in one direction: discovery, questions and checkout, without leaving TikTok.

## What TikTok announced

**Buy Direct.** An in-app checkout. According to TikTok, users can buy from a brand without leaving the app, from the For You feed with a single click.

**Shopping Assistant.** A conversational AI agent that, TikTok says, remembers what a user needs and gives real-time guidance on product details, shipping, sizing, availability and purchasing in one conversation.

**Agentic Leads.** An AI agent for lead generation that "will be available" as a Lead Agent in TikTok Direct Messages and in lead forms on advertisers' own websites.

**TikTok Ad Network for US advertisers.** Campaigns can extend beyond TikTok to a network of **nearly 400,000 apps** worldwide, managed inside TikTok Ads Manager.

**TikTok for Business MCP as a connector.** TikTok's ads interface is now available inside AI platforms including Claude, Perplexity, Replit and Manus. TikTok says the number of advertisers using the MCP has risen by **over 200%** since launch, based on internal data. It didn't give a starting number, so treat that figure carefully.

## The catch

PPC Land pointed out that the announcement contains **no pricing and no dated rollout schedule** for any of the new items. Buy Direct, for example, has no stated start date, no list of markets and no detail on what buyer data reaches the brand.

So this is a direction of travel, not a switch you can flip tomorrow.

## Why it matters for marketers

For years the social commerce funnel looked like this: video, profile, link, website, cart, checkout. Every step lost people. TikTok is trying to collapse that into: video, one click.

If it works, two things change:

1. **Your product page data matters more than your landing page design.** An AI assistant answering "will this fit?" needs clear sizing, shipping and stock information to work with.
2. **Creative becomes the checkout.** The video isn't the top of the funnel any more. It might be the whole funnel.

## What I'd do

- **Audit your product data.** Sizes, materials, delivery times, returns. Write them clearly, in one place.
- **Prepare a FAQ for the assistant era.** List the ten questions customers ask your support team before buying. Make sure every answer is public.
- **Test the ad network carefully.** If you're a US advertiser, start with a small budget and compare results to in-feed placements.
- **Try the MCP connector for reporting first.** Asking an assistant to summarise campaign performance is a low-risk way to learn the tool.
- **Don't bet the quarter on undated features.** Plan for them. Budget for them when they have a date.

Having worked on 850+ creator deals, I've seen how often a great video lost the sale at the link in bio. One-click checkout from the feed goes straight at that problem. I'll believe the impact when brands report results.

## Sources

article:
## YouTube is handing viewers the remote for their homepage

At **Made On YouTube 2026** on 23 September, YouTube announced more than a few AI features. For marketers, one stands out: **Custom Feeds**.

## What Custom Feeds are

According to YouTube's official blog, Custom Feeds will let users in the US "curate your homepage based on specific moods or interests." It's coming to web, mobile and TVs this fall.

Social Media Today described how it works: a viewer creates a feed with a prompt, and that feed then lives as a tab at the top of their homepage. So someone could have a tab for quick dinner recipes, another for marathon training, another for B2B marketing breakdowns.

YouTube also highlighted Ask YouTube for instant recommendations. Put together, the direction is clear: viewers are getting more ways to say what they want in plain language.

## Why this changes the job

Until now, the YouTube homepage has been one feed per person, shaped mostly by what they watched before. You competed to look like the next sensible video.

With Custom Feeds, a viewer can describe an intent directly. That shifts the question from "does my video resemble what this person watched?" to "does my video clearly match what this person asked for?"

That's a familiar shift for anyone who has followed AI search. When a prompt sorts the content, clarity about topic and audience matters more.

## What we don't know

I want to be honest about the limits. YouTube hasn't explained how Custom Feeds choose videos, what signals they rely on, or whether ads appear inside them. It's US only at first. So anyone telling you exactly how to "rank in Custom Feeds" today is guessing.

What we can say is that a video with a vague title and an empty description gives any system less to work with.

## What I'd do

- **Say who the video is for, early.** In the title, the first line of the description and the first seconds of the video.
- **Name the problem in plain words.** The words a viewer would type, not your internal campaign name.
- **Use chapters.** They describe what's inside the video in a structured way.
- **Build series around clear interests.** A playlist on one topic is easier to match to a mood or interest than a random mix.
- **Watch your traffic sources.** When Custom Feeds roll out, check YouTube Analytics for changes in where views come from, before changing strategy.

From my creator marketing work, the channels that held up through every algorithm change were the ones with a clear promise. Custom Feeds look like another reward for that.

article:
## The 2% problem nobody puts on a slide

Andreessen Horowitz's **State of Markets II** report has two numbers that belong together, and both are about 2%.

1. **About 2% of US households** were paying for an AI service as of April.
2. **Only about 2% of S&P 500 companies** reported a tracked AI metric, even though nearly 30% reported some quantifiable AI impact.

The report was highlighted by Cointelegraph on 2 October and covered by Crypto Briefing.

## The consumer number

The household figure is the one getting headlines. a16z says paid adoption has risen since April but remains a small share of households. It didn't give an updated percentage.

That's a useful reality check for anyone building or marketing an AI product to consumers. Usage is not the same as willingness to pay. Free tiers are doing a lot of the work.

## The business number matters more

For marketers, the more interesting figure is the corporate one. Nearly 30% of S&P 500 companies report some quantifiable AI impact. Only about 2% report a tracked metric.

Put simply: plenty of large companies say AI is helping. Very few show a number they consistently measure. a16z described overall adoption as broad but relatively shallow.

I'd be careful not to over-read this. "Tracked metric" is a high bar for public reporting, and many companies may track things internally without disclosing them. But the gap between claims and evidence is real, and most marketing teams I know recognise it.

## Why this is an opportunity

If you work in marketing, this is good news. The person who can prove an AI result is rare. That makes them valuable.

You don't need a data science team to do it. You need a before number, an after number and a record of how you got them. That's an operations habit, not a technical skill.

It's also why I'm moving towards AI Ops. The tools are getting easier. The measurement is still mostly missing.

## What I'd do

- **Pick one repeatable task.** A weekly report, a content brief, ad variations, a newsletter draft.
- **Time it for two weeks without AI.** Write down the hours and the quality issues.
- **Run it for two weeks with AI.** Same task, same person, same quality check.
- **Track one quality measure too.** Edit rounds, error count, or a performance metric like click rate. Speed alone can hide worse work.
- **Write a one-paragraph summary.** What changed, by how much, and what still needs a human.
- **Share it internally.** One honest, measured result beats ten enthusiastic anecdotes.

If you're a founder selling AI to consumers, the takeaway is different: plan for a long free tier and a narrow path to paying users. Your marketing has to show a result people would pay for, not just a demo they enjoy.

## Sources

- [Bloomingbit: report on a16z household AI spending (via Cointelegraph)](https://en.bloomingbit.io/feed/news/121506)

article:
## Google's AI Max now speaks seven more languages

On 23 September, Google announced two updates for **AI Max for Search**, its AI driven Search campaign feature.

1. The closed beta of **AI Brief** is expanding to **Dutch, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese and Spanish**.
2. A new **unified reporting** view for the Search ads journey.

For European advertisers, the first one matters a lot.

## What AI Brief does

In Google's words, AI Brief "lets you guide AI Max in your own words with detailed context on your business, audience, and key messaging."

In practice, it's a written brief for the machine. Instead of only feeding the system keywords, assets and a URL, you tell it who you serve, what you offer and what you want to say. Until now, that was limited in language. Now advertisers can write it in seven more languages, including German and French.

It's still a **closed beta**, so not every account will see it.

## The new report

Google is also introducing a reporting feature that shows a single view of the Search ads journey:

- which **search terms** triggered your ads
- which **creative assets** the user saw
- where they **landed** on your website

That's useful because AI Max decides a lot on its own, from matching to creative. Seeing the full path in one place makes it easier to check whether the AI's choices make sense for your business. Google hasn't announced when the report will be generally available.

## Why the brief is becoming the main asset

When AI picks the queries and assembles the ads, your control shifts upstream. The brief is where your strategy lives now. A good brief is specific about audience, offer and boundaries. A weak one gives the AI room to guess.

That's also why language matters. A German brief can use the actual words German customers search with, instead of a translation of an English idea.

## What I'd do

- **Write the brief in your customers' language,** not your head office's language.
- **Include what you don't want.** Products you don't sell, claims you can't make, audiences that aren't a fit.
- **Name your top three messages.** In priority order, in plain words.
- **Add proof points.** Delivery times, guarantees, certifications. Real ones only.
- **Review the new report monthly** once it's available: search term, creative, landing page. If any link in that chain looks wrong, fix the brief first.

My limit: I don't have access data for this beta, so I can't tell you how much a brief changes results. Treat it as a test with a control period.

article:
## Made On YouTube 2026, filtered for creators and brands

On 23 September, YouTube announced its yearly batch of product updates at **Made On YouTube 2026**. There's a lot in there. Here are the five updates I think matter most for creators and the brands that work with them.

## 1. An AI editing assistant you talk to

YouTube is integrating Gemini into a **conversational editing assistant** for Shorts and the YouTube Create app. According to YouTube, creators can use text prompts to **trim speech, sync music, add text hooks and reorder frames**.

TechCrunch reports the tool should be available early next year. So this is coming, not here.

Why it matters: the boring parts of short-form editing are exactly the parts that slow creators down. If a prompt can tighten the first three seconds and add a hook, more creators can publish more often.

## 2. Shorts series

Creators can now structure Shorts into **seasons and episodes**, making episodic storytelling and microdramas easier to watch on mobile and TV.

For brands, that opens a format beyond the single sponsored video: a short branded series with a story that carries across episodes.

## 3. Likeness detection for face and voice

YouTube says creators can **protect their voice and face with expanded likeness detection**. As AI generated copies of real people get easier to make, this is becoming a practical safety tool, not a niche feature.

## 4. Getting noticed by brands

YouTube also highlighted ways for creators to **get noticed by brands and find resources for pitching partnerships**. Details are still emerging, but the direction is clear: YouTube wants more of the brand deal process to happen on YouTube.

## 5. Live auto-dubbing

Live streamers get **real-time auto-dubbing** to break language barriers. For creators with international audiences, a live Q&A or product launch could reach viewers who don't speak the creator's language.

## What it means for brand partnerships

From my work across 850+ creator deals, three practical changes follow:

- **Contracts need likeness terms.** Who can use the creator's face and voice, for how long, and whether AI versions are allowed. Write it down.
- **Briefs can ask for series, not one-offs.** A three-episode Shorts arc may tell your story better than one 60-second ad.
- **Production timelines may shrink.** If editing gets faster, plan for quicker turnarounds, but keep review steps.

## What I'd do

- Creators: register for likeness detection as soon as it's available to you.
- Brands: add an AI and likeness clause to your next creator contract.
- Both: sketch one Shorts series idea now, so you're ready when your audience starts watching in episodes.

My limit: several of these features roll out over the coming months, and some may arrive in the US first. Check availability in your market before planning around them.
